title: Bus-Sized Asteroid 2026 VJ13 Passes Earth Tuesday; Four Days of Data Pin Timing Within One Minute
excerpt: Asteroid passing Earth on Tuesday, 2026 VJ13, is a bus-sized near-Earth asteroid that NASA JPL and ESA say will pass about 837,000 miles away at 12:35 a.m. ET, with timing good to under one minute after only four days of tracking. ESA’s risk list excludes it, and brightness data allow a size
content:
Bus-sized asteroid 2026 VJ13 will pass Earth at about 12:35 a.m. ET on Tuesday, Nov. 17, at roughly 837,000 miles, or 3.5 times the average Earth-Moon distance of about 239,000 miles, according to NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) and the European Space Agency (ESA). Astronomers have tracked the object for only four days, yet both agencies put the uncertainty in its pass time at under one minute.

The flyby needs no response from anyone: 2026 VJ13 is far too small to qualify as hazardous, and ESA's risk list does not include it. What it shows is how much a short run of telescope measurements can pin down, and what it cannot. JPL's Asteroid Watch dashboard lists only a date for the pass, so the clock time and error bars below come from JPL's close-approach database and ESA's Near-Earth Object Coordination Centre.

Five Approaches in Two Days: 2026 VW15 Has Passed, 2026 VJ13 Arrives at 12:35 AM ET

JPL's Asteroid Watch dashboard lists five approaches across Nov. 16 and 17, each inside the dashboard's cutoff of 4.6 million miles, or about 19.5 times the Moon's distance. According to JPL close-approach data, 2026 VW15 already passed at about 12:26 a.m. ET Monday, 2026 VM3 will pass at about 11:47 a.m. ET today, and the other three follow early Tuesday.

Lunar distances, Eastern Time conversions and mph speeds in the table are TechTimes calculations from JPL and CNEOS figures.

The largest object in the group, 2026 VB13, is about 98 feet across and passes nearly three times farther away than 2026 VJ13, at roughly twice its speed. The last entry, 2023 VE6, has been known since 2023: its "V" marks Nov. 1 to 15 of that year, and the "E" and cycle number 6 make it the 155th object logged in that half-month. Its listed time is nominal, because JPL's database carries a 3-sigma pass-time uncertainty of about five days for this object.

Four Days of Observations Fix 2026 VJ13's Pass Time to Under One Minute

JPL's Small-Body Database shows 32 observations spanning Nov. 12 to Nov. 16, which is the entire basis for the object's orbit. The designation fits that timeline: the "V" in 2026 VJ13 marks Nov. 1 to 15, and the "J" with cycle number 13 makes it the 334th object logged in that half-month.

From those four days, JPL computes an Apollo-class orbit, meaning the object's path crosses Earth's. The rock circles the Sun every 951 days, about 2.6 years, ranging from roughly 84 million miles to 268 million miles from the Sun.

JPL's close-approach table and ESA both place the pass at about 12:35 a.m. ET. JPL gives a 3-sigma time uncertainty of under one minute, and ESA likewise lists an uncertainty under one minute. The 3-sigma distance bounds run from about 834,600 miles to 839,500 miles, an error band roughly 5,000 miles wide around the nominal 837,000 miles.

Why can a short run of data do that? The Minor Planet Center grades orbit uncertainty by how many arcseconds an object's predicted position drifts per decade. Because error grows the farther a prediction reaches beyond the observations, a pass days after the last measurement sits at the tightest end of the error budget.

JPL Lists No Return Within 18.6 Million Miles Through 2099, on Four Days of Data

JPL's close-approach database returns no further pass by 2026 VJ13 inside 0.2 astronomical units, about 18.6 million miles, between Nov. 18, 2026 and the end of 2099. That table rests on the same four-day orbit, and JPL's current solution is dated Nov. 16. The Minor Planet Center also warns that its uncertainty grade is not a guide to how well a near-Earth asteroid's future motion is known. A confident forecast for this Tuesday does not carry over to far-future dates until more observations arrive.

How Big Is Asteroid 2026 VJ13? Brightness Data Allow 24 to 82 Feet

JPL's dashboard lists 2026 VJ13 at about 39 feet, but that figure starts from brightness, not a direct measurement. JPL's database gives the asteroid's absolute magnitude, a brightness rating, as 27.242, with an uncertainty of 0.368. Turning that into a diameter requires assuming how much sunlight the surface reflects. Catalogs commonly assume 14%, while real asteroid reflectivity can range from at least 5% to 30%, so estimates can be off by more than a factor of two.

A TechTimes calculation using the standard brightness-to-diameter conversion shows the spread. At 14% reflectivity, 2026 VJ13 comes out near 12.6 meters (41 feet), close to JPL's figure. At 5% reflectivity it grows to 21.2 meters (69 feet), and at 30% it shrinks to 8.6 meters (28 feet). Stacking the brightness uncertainty on top gives a full range of 7.3 to 25.1 meters (24 to 82 feet). A tracker fed by CNEOS data lists 10 to 21 meters (33 to 69 feet). Even the top of that range sits far below the size at which asteroids count as hazardous.

Bus-Size Rocks Pass Several Times Yearly, MIT's Richard Binzel Says; 2026 JH2 Surfaced Eight Days Out

Richard Binzel, a planetary scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and creator of the Torino Scale, told CNN in May that car-sized objects pass between Earth and the Moon every week and that school-bus-sized ones come through Earth's neighborhood several times per year.

The May flyby of 2026 JH2 shows the pattern. The Mount Lemmon Survey in Arizona discovered it on May 10, and it passed on May 18 at about 56,913 miles, roughly 24% of the Moon's distance. ESA put its width at 14 to 30 meters (46 to 98 feet). An even smaller object, 2026 JN4, about 0.63 to 1.4 meters (2.1 to 4.6 feet) across, was flagged before it entered the atmosphere over the Arafura Sea on May 15, the 12th impactor predicted in advance.

The catalog keeps growing. ESA's July newsletter counted 41,958 known near-Earth asteroids and 1,429 near-Earth objects discovered since Jan. 1, and said it expects rapid growth in most of those figures as LSST operations begin. One tracking site counted 118 asteroids that had passed within one lunar distance of Earth in 2026 as of Sept. 21; 2026 VJ13 will pass well outside that line, at 3.5 lunar distances.

Larger rocks remain the bigger gap. NASA's planetary defense office lists 11,343 near-Earth asteroids larger than 140 meters (459 feet) as found, with an estimated 14,000 still to be discovered, as of Dec. 3, 2025. Peter Brown of Western University in Canada puts the rate of car-sized rocks entering the atmosphere at roughly once a year and house-sized ones at every few decades. For scale, the 2013 Chelyabinsk object was about 18 meters (59 feet) across, was not detected beforehand, and left 1,491 people seeking medical treatment, mostly from broken glass.

Does 2026 VJ13 Count as Potentially Hazardous? Size Rule Says No by Wide Margin

NASA's CNEOS classes an asteroid as potentially hazardous only if its minimum orbit intersection distance, the gap between its orbit and Earth's, is 0.05 astronomical units (about 4.65 million miles) or less and its absolute magnitude is 22.0 or brighter, which corresponds to roughly 140 meters (459 feet) across. JPL's database lists that distance for 2026 VJ13 at 0.0088 astronomical units, about 818,000 miles, which falls inside the distance limit. The size test fails by a wide margin: at 27.242, its absolute magnitude is 5.2 steps fainter than the cutoff, which works out to roughly 11 times smaller in diameter at the same reflectivity, by TechTimes calculation. JPL's database flags 2026 VJ13 as not potentially hazardous.

The dashboard applies a similar yardstick, noting that objects larger than about 150 meters (492 feet) that come within its cutoff distance count as potentially hazardous. None of the five approaches reaches that size, and the largest, 2026 VB13, is about 98 feet (30 meters).

For readers, the practical takeaways are simple. The pass poses no threat, its time and distance are firm to the minute and to a few thousand miles, its size is an estimate with wide error bars, and any claim about this rock's distant future rests on four days of observations.

Frequently Asked Questions

How can astronomers time a pass to the minute after only four days of data?

Orbit error grows with time. The Minor Planet Center grades orbit uncertainty by the arcseconds of position drift per decade, so a pass days after the observations falls at the tightest end of that budget, while predictions decades out are far looser.

Is asteroid 2026 VJ13 dangerous, and will it come back?

It is not classed as potentially hazardous, and ESA's risk list does not include it. JPL's close-approach database shows no other pass within about 18.6 million miles through 2099 on the current orbit, a solution built from four days of observations that can change as more arrive.

Why do trackers list different sizes for asteroid 2026 VJ13?

Each estimate starts from brightness and then assumes how reflective the surface is. JPL's dashboard says about 39 feet, a CNEOS-fed tracker says 10 to 21 meters (33 to 69 feet), and TechTimes' full-range calculation gives 24 to 82 feet.

Are bus-sized asteroids passing Earth common?

Yes. According to CNN's interview with Binzel, school-bus-sized objects come through Earth's neighborhood several times a year, and one tracking site had counted 118 asteroids within one lunar distance of Earth in 2026 by Sept. 21.
